headline: Cambodia's Irrawaddy Dolphins Show Signs of Recovery
meta_description: Six calves born this year bring hope to Cambodia's endangered Irrawaddy dolphins as conservation efforts strengthen along the Mekong River.
summary_short: Six Irrawaddy dolphin calves were born in Cambodia this year, increasing the population to 118 and signaling that the species can recover with proper protection.
body:
For the first time in years, the future of the Mekong River's Irrawaddy dolphins looks a little brighter. Six calves were confirmed to be born this year in Cambodia, swelling the population to 118 individuals—a modest but meaningful increase for a species that has teetered on the edge of collapse. The births suggest that if dolphins and their habitats receive sustained protection, the species can rebound from decades of steep decline. The news arrives at a critical moment: the Irrawaddy dolphin population in Cambodia's stretch of the Mekong has plummeted from around 200 individuals in the late 1990s to just over 100 today, driven by hunting, entanglement in fishing nets, and habitat degradation. One neighboring pool, the Anlong Chheu Teal pool along the Laos-Cambodia border, offers a sobering reminder of what failure looks like—its last dolphin died in 2022, and tourism revenue that once sustained local communities collapsed entirely.

These gray cetaceans hold profound significance for Mekong communities. Local boatmen like Heang Koeurn, who has watched for dolphins every morning for 11 years, depend on tourists drawn to see the animals breaking the surface of the water. But the dolphins mean far more than income: Cambodian and Laotian communities regard them as sacred, representing ancestral spirits of the river itself. River guards and conservation workers now focus their efforts on the three deep pools that shelter the remaining population, including the 60-meter-deep Kampi pool in Kratie province. In 2022 alone, authorities confiscated 36,000 meters of illegal gillnets—a testament to the constant pressure these mammals face. What gives hope is that this year's births prove survival is possible when communities, government, and enforcement work together to keep illegal fishing methods at bay.
quick_facts: Six calves born in Cambodia in 2024, raising population to 118
Population dropped from ~200 in late 1990s to just over 100
Kampi pool in Kratie province is 60 meters deep, main habitat
36,000 meters of illegal gillnets confiscated in 2022 alone
Last dolphin in Anlong Chheu Teal pool died in 2022
